newsitem.title: INDIA: Ex-India PM plays key role in crisis from hospital.
newsitem.headline: Ex-India PM plays key role in crisis from hospital.

text.p: Former prime minister Vishwanath Pratap Singh, whose 11-month tenure in 1989 and 1990 altered the face of Indian politics, is playing a central role in efforts to defuse a political crisis from a hospital bed.
Since the turmoil erupted one week ago, Singh has received a virtually uninterrupted string of visitors in his room in Delhi's Apollo Hospital where he is being treated for kidney trouble.
One of the latest visitors was Congress party president Sitaram Kesri, who came to see Singh late on Saturday.
Kesri sparked the political turmoil on March 30 when he abruptly announced his party was withdrawing its vital support for Prime Minister H.D. Deve Gowda.
"The talks were good, but not something to be disclosed," Kesri told reporters after meeting Singh.

The visitors, captured on film by a phalanx of media crews, say they come to enquire about Singh's health. But it is one of New Delhi's worst-kept secrets that the health of the government is at least as much on their minds.

The government faces a confidence vote set for April 11. Politicians in Congress and Deve Gowda's United Front coalition are striving to avoid a mid-term poll after last year's inconclusive elections that threw up a hung parliament.
"As long as there is desire, there is hope," the frail, bespectacled Singh told a television reporter on Saturday from his hospital bed.

Singh has met not just his own followers in the United Front, but also former prime minister P.V. Narasimha Rao, Kesri's main party rival, and other Congress leaders believed to be upset with Kesri's sudden attack.
Kesri says Deve Gowda must resign for Congress to resume its backing. The United Front has rejected the demand.

Until last month, the Congress had offered make-or-break support to Deve Gowda which allowed the United Front to oust a 12-day-old government headed by the Bharatiya Janata Party (BJP), its arch-rival.
The Hindu nationalist BJP is the largest group in India's 542-member lower house of parliament which will vote on Friday.
Singh is seen as having the capacity to influence leaders of both the United Front and Congress.
"Now only the Congress MPs can avert elections and thereby save the situation," Singh was quoted on Sunday as saying.

Singh had a controversial tenure in office until November 1990. When he was in power the BJP launched a campaign to build a temple in the town of Ayodhya. In December 1992, Hindu zealots demolished a 16th century mosque at the site, sparking nationwide riots.
Singh's National Front coalition lost the BJP's support in October 1990 after he cracked down on its campaign.
Weeks before, Singh had implemented affirmative job quotas in government for lower-caste Hindus. The move provoked a backlash from mainly upper-caste students who feared for their future.
The events of 1990 strengthened Singh's Janata Dal, which headed the National Front, and also the BJP, which scored huge electoral gains on the strength of its religious campaign.
Later, Singh, citing health as a reason, opted out of electoral politics, but last year helped form the United Front, in which communists joined former National Front parties.
